catalog_quote: Many monosyllabic words have long vowels in all contexts. Most open syllable monosyllabic words have vowel length when spoken in isolation. In this latter case, the length is nonphonemic. There are also other examples of nonphonemic length. Often the vowels of stressed syllables are slightly lengthened and, as an intonational feature, the vowel in the peak syllable of an utterance is often lengthened. ... 6. TONE AND INTGNATIQN ... audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: all fragments of the deciding quotation and the domain quote are verbatim in the scanned file we hold at the stated sections/lines; archive.org metadata confirms the item is Kilpatrick 1985, OPSL 4. (2) The deciding source is a dedicated descriptive phonology (62 pp) with a full tone chapter; it is the primary phonology in Glottolog's list (the 1979 entry is its unpublished draft). (3) I downloaded the three later SIL-South Sudan descriptions (Grammar Book 2018, 345 pp; Consonant and Vowel Book 2018, 72 pp; Dictionary 2018) from webonary: all analyse Bongo with five underlying lexical tone patterns on noun roots and tonal verb morphology, and none contains the word 'stress' or 'accent', which independently confirms the tonal coding with no stress rule. sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'There are five different patterns of tone in Bongo nouns' (H, L, LH, LHL, HL, e.g. maya 'yam' LHL vs maya 'milk' L); syllables = 'beats', no prominence mentioned; fn. 3: 'Without further tone analysis, there is not much solid evidence for a vowel length distinction' (long vowels mostly in monosyllables). No mention of stress or accent anywhere.
sources.locator: 'Tone' lesson p. 41 (extracted text); vowel-length lesson p. 34 with fn. 3; syllables lesson p. 6

sources.citation: Moi, Daniel Rabbi et al. (with Tim Stirtz, SIL). 2018. Bongo-English Dictionary. 48 pp. Juba: SIL-South Sudan (webonary.org/bongo).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'Tone is the high, low, falling or rising sound of a word. There are five different patterns of tone in Bongo nouns' with counts per underlying pattern (e.g. L: 103 two-beat nouns); surface vs underlying tone marked in entries. No stress/accent statement.

Bongo Grammar Book. Third Trial Edition, 345 pp. Juba: SIL-South Sudan. (Glottolog 470694 lists the 2014 first trial ed., 224 pp.)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'Tone is the high, low, falling or rising sound of a word ... Noun roots with 2 beats have one of five underlying tones (or tone patterns): H, L, LH, LHL or HL'; verb roots with 1 beat H, L, LH, LHL; tone alone distinguishes complete/incomplete verbs in some cases. Zero occurrences of 'stress' or 'accent' in 345 pp.
sources.locator: lesson 'Underlying and surface tone' p. 153 ff. (extracted text); whole-text a full-text search for stress/accent

sources.note: Longest grammar of Bongo before the SIL trial books; missionary grammars of this era often carry an explicit 'accent' paragraph, which would be the only place a stress-placement claim for Bongo could exist. Unlikely to overturn a tonal coding.
